name: wasmga.me
tagline: Retro and console games running in the browser via WebAssembly, with a hosted library and cloud saves.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The part that looks hard, running a console emulator in a browser tab, is the part someone else already solved: libretro cores compiled to WebAssembly ship as a package you can drop into a static site in an afternoon. An agent can give you a game grid, a fullscreen canvas, gamepad mapping, save states in IndexedDB and a save export button in one sitting. What it cannot give you is the library, because the catalog is content someone either licensed or hosts at their own risk, and you will be supplying your own dumps either way. Mobile touch controls, per-core tuning and cross-device save sync are the gaps that turn one sitting into a weekend. If you already have a ROM folder and one device, the personal build is honestly fine.
coreLoopDIY: A static site that loads WebAssembly emulator cores, boots game files you dropped in yourself, and keeps save states and SRAM in browser storage with file export.
requirements: Your own legally dumped game files, nothing is bundled
Prebuilt WebAssembly emulator cores, you are not writing an emulator
A static host or just a local dev server
A reasonably fast machine for anything past the 16-bit era
BIOS files for the cores that need them
whatYouLose: A ready-made catalog you can click into without sourcing anything
Cloud save sync across phone, laptop and someone else's browser
Touch controls and mobile layouts that actually work one-handed
Per-game core settings, shaders and compatibility fixes someone else already debugged
Any argument that what you are doing is licensed
moatNotes: The emulator is free software. The library, the licensing posture and the per-game compatibility notes are the asset, and none of that compiles.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the appeal is opening a tab and playing, not assembling a ROM set, chasing BIOS files and discovering that your core runs at 40fps on a laptop. A hosted service absorbs the sourcing problem, the compatibility problem and the sync problem, and if it is actually licensing titles it absorbs the legal problem too. A self-hosted build is cheaper and yours, but it starts empty and stays empty until you fill it.
notes: The emulation is a dependency install; the hard parts are the ones no prompt can fetch for you.
prompt:
Build a local-first browser game console: a static web app that runs WebAssembly emulator cores on game files the user supplies.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + TypeScript + React, no backend, no server code at all.
- EmulatorJS vendored into /public/emulator as static files, loaded from the same origin. Do not fetch cores from a CDN at runtime.
- Tailwind for styling. idb-keyval for IndexedDB.
- Deployable as plain static files to any host or opened from a local dev server.

In scope:
- A library screen: grid of game cards with cover art placeholder, title, system, last played.
- Drag and drop or file picker to add game files. Detect the system from the file extension, let the user override it with a dropdown. Store the file bytes in IndexedDB keyed by a content hash, store metadata separately.
- A player screen: fullscreen-capable canvas, EmulatorJS booted with the right core for the detected system.
- Save state slots: four per game, written to IndexedDB. Buttons to save, load, and delete each slot. Also persist SRAM on exit.
- Export and import: dump all metadata and save states to a single .zip the user downloads, and restore from that zip. This is the only sync mechanism.
- Keyboard mapping screen plus Gamepad API support with a remap flow that reads live button presses.
- A BIOS slot per system, stored the same way as games, with a clear message when a core needs one and it is missing.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Accounts, auth, telemetry, analytics, any network call beyond loading local assets.
- A game catalog, ROM downloads, scraping, or any bundled content. The library starts empty and says so.
- Writing an emulator. Use the prebuilt cores.
- Mobile touch overlays. Note in the README that this is desktop and gamepad only for now.

Details:
- Put any configurable paths in .env, commit .env.example only.
- Warn clearly if storage quota is close to full, and show total bytes used in settings.
- README: how to vendor EmulatorJS, which systems the included cores cover, where BIOS files go, and a plain statement that the user supplies their own game files.
- Ship with one empty-state screen that explains the whole flow in three steps.
